Theorist.structural_strength: The paper uses a disciplined common-model comparison: ten policy rules are evaluated in the same FRB/US environment, with identical shock resampling, neutral-rate assumptions, ELB constraint, performance statistics, and two explicitly distinguished expectation specifications. The aggregate-demand-shock exercise usefully explains the stochastic rankings through the economic tradeoff between insufficient ELB accommodation and excessive post-ELB overshooting.
Theorist.domain_audit: The central result is valid only under a narrower interpretation than the manuscript gives it. MCAP is not a general model of imperfect policy credibility: asset-market participants fully understand and believe the new rule, while nonfinancial expectations come from a small VAR and are imposed not to change with the rule. Moreover, MCAP is motivated as describing a transition, but reported observations begin after a 100-quarter burn-in and cover another 100 quarters, with no learning by nonfinancial agents. Consequently, the simulations establish robustness to one specific, persistent hybrid-expectations stress test, not that lower-for-longer policies generally remain advantageous under imperfect credibility or during regime transitions. This does not invalidate the conditional FRB/US rankings, but it materially narrows the headline interpretation.
Theorist.best_case_contribution: Within FRB/US, under a three-percent neutral nominal rate and the manuscript's two expectation specifications, the paper shows that lower-for-longer rules are not interchangeable. Short-memory temporary price-level targeting and shadow-rate rules balance ELB stimulus against subsequent overshooting better than ordinary Taylor rules or flexible price-level targeting. This is a useful quantitative policy comparison because it identifies policy designs whose rankings survive a deliberately unfavorable failure of nonfinancial expectations to adjust.
Theorist.minimum_viable_revision: Recast MCAP throughout as a particular hybrid or invariant-expectations stress test rather than a general representation of imperfect credibility or transition dynamics. Narrow the principal conclusion accordingly, explain that the long simulations do not model learning or convergence after regime adoption, and distinguish credibility of the announced rule from agents' forecasting technology. The existing numerical results can remain unchanged. A stronger but nonminimal revision would parameterize partial credibility or gradual learning within the same FRB/US framework.
Theorist.severity_rationale: The simulations appear internally interpretable as outcomes under imposed heterogeneous forecasting rules, so the concern is not a demonstrated mathematical error. However, the manuscript's principal finding is expressly framed as applying to imperfect credibility, whereas only one extreme and persistent expectation specification is examined. Narrowing the claim from general credibility robustness to robustness under MCAP materially changes the policy contribution, making this a central rephrasing issue rather than a minor qualification. It can be repaired without changing the model or results.

novelty_claims.description: The paper quantitatively compares multiple lower-for-longer designs in FRB/US and argues that short-memory temporary price-level targeting and shadow-rate rules remain superior to traditional Taylor rules even when nonfinancial expectations do not adjust to the policy regime.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The manuscript compares ten rules in Tables 1 and 2 under MCE and MCAP. The component methods and policy ideas are largely inherited: Kiley and Roberts (2017) provide closely related simulations under MCE; Reifschneider and Roberts (2006) discuss the expectation assumptions; Bernanke (2017) discusses temporary price-level targeting; and Reifschneider-Williams and Kiley-Roberts supply the shadow-rate rules. The genuine new ingredient is the common quantitative comparison of these policy designs across the two expectation specifications, not a new equilibrium mechanism or simulation method.

insight_assessment.description: The argument is clear and economically useful: robust ELB policy must provide enough accommodation during the downturn without generating destabilizing output and inflation overshoots afterward. The paper connects this intuition to the rule rankings and the aggregate-demand-shock exercise. The exposition is competent rather than exceptional because the exact transmission mechanisms and rule equations are deferred to an online appendix, and the economic distinction between credibility, bounded expectations, and learning is insufficiently developed.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Section IV states that robust frameworks share two characteristics: sufficient stimulus at the ELB and avoidance of excessively large overshoots after liftoff. Figure 1 is used to contrast the inertial Taylor rule, inertial flexible price-level targeting, and one-year-memory temporary price-level targeting. Tables 1 and 2 then show how the same tradeoff appears in stochastic losses.

Theorist.layman_translation: The simulations offer a useful lesson: promising to keep rates low after a recession can help, but promises that compensate for too much past inflation weakness may overheat the economy later. The best-performing rules in this model use limited memory or track forgone rate cuts. The caveat is that the paper has tested only one unusual form of limited public belief—financial markets understand the new policy perfectly, while households and firms never revise their forecasting rule—so it cannot yet claim that the findings hold for imperfect credibility in general.
Theorist.source_evidence: The manuscript defines MCE as a case in which all private agents understand and believe the monetary policy rule. It defines MCAP as a case in which asset prices are forward-looking but expectations of income, inflation, and other nonfinancial variables are based on a small VAR and are 'assumed not to change when the policy rule changes.' It then says MCAP 'better describes the situation during a transition to a new policy rule.' Yet Section I reports 200-quarter simulations, discards the first 100 quarters as burn-in, and evaluates the second 100 quarters without any stated learning mechanism. The conclusion generalizes from this setup to the claim that 'imperfect credibility of the policy regime reduces but does not eliminate the advantages' of lower-for-longer policies. Tables 1 and 2 support the narrower conditional result: one-year-memory temporary price-level targeting lowers loss from 17.2 to 8.5 under MCE and from 15.2 to 10.7 under MCAP relative to the non-inertial Taylor rule, while flexible price-level targeting performs especially poorly under MCAP.

CS_Expert.structural_strength: The computational experiment is conceptually well structured: the authors hold the FRB/US model, neutral nominal rate, inflation target, shock history, simulation length, and evaluation criteria fixed while varying policy rules and two expectations regimes. Reporting ELB frequency and duration, target biases, RMSDs, and a common loss function makes the broad policy comparisons transparent.
CS_Expert.domain_audit: The numerical results are not independently reproducible from the manuscript. The paper says it uses 500 bootstrapped FRB/US simulations, but it does not provide the FRB/US vintage and coefficient set, executable code, exact equations for the ten rules, residual data, random seed, bootstrap dependence structure, initialization procedure, rational-expectations solution method, convergence criteria, or treatment of failed simulations. Several essential definitions are deferred to an unavailable online appendix. In particular, saying that the authors bootstrap model residuals does not establish whether residual vectors are resampled jointly across equations, whether temporal blocks are used, or how the 1970-2015 residual history is aligned. These choices can materially alter shock covariance, ELB incidence, tail behavior, and the ranking of rules. The manuscript also gives no Monte Carlo standard errors, so close comparisons such as losses of 8.0 versus 8.5 under MCE cannot be distinguished from simulation noise. This does not demonstrate that the reported calculations are incorrect, but the central quantitative evidence cannot be audited or executed under the stated inputs.
CS_Expert.best_case_contribution: The strongest credible contribution is a controlled FRB/US simulation comparison showing that some lower-for-longer strategies—especially short-memory temporary price-level targeting and shadow-rate rules—remain superior to conventional Taylor rules even when nonfinancial private expectations do not adjust to the new regime. The comparison usefully identifies a policy-design tradeoff between adequate ELB stimulus and post-ELB overshooting.
CS_Expert.minimum_viable_revision: Provide a complete computational replication package or an equivalently detailed executable specification: identify the exact FRB/US vintage and data, state every policy-rule equation and state variable, document the MCE and MCAP solution algorithms, publish the residual series and joint or block-bootstrap procedure, specify seeds and initial conditions, report convergence and simulation-failure diagnostics, and include code that recreates Tables 1 and 2. Add Monte Carlo standard errors or repeated-seed intervals for all reported statistics and qualify rankings whose differences are not numerically distinguishable.
CS_Expert.severity_rationale: The paper's central findings are quantitative rankings generated entirely by a complex stochastic simulation pipeline. Because the manuscript does not specify that pipeline sufficiently to reproduce or audit it, the tables cannot presently substantiate the policy ranking independently. Implementation and resampling choices could change ELB frequencies, volatility, and close loss comparisons. The defect is serious but repairable within the existing framework by releasing the computational specification, replication materials, and simulation-uncertainty diagnostics; it is therefore a REVISION rather than a BLOCKER.

novelty_claims.description: The paper extends existing lower-for-longer policy comparisons by evaluating a broad suite of temporary price-level-targeting and shadow-rate rules in FRB/US under both full model-consistent expectations and an imperfect-credibility regime in which only asset-market participants understand the policy rule.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The manuscript identifies Kiley and Roberts (2017) as using the MCE assumption and describes its added MCAP exercises as representing transition to a new regime. The new ingredient is the systematic robustness comparison across expectations regimes, not a new model or simulation method. The paper itself notes that Hebden and Lopez-Salido (2018) already consider several lower-for-longer approaches under MCE.

insight_assessment.description: The argument has a clear economic architecture: low neutral rates increase ELB exposure; lower-for-longer policies operate through expectations and asset prices; imperfect credibility weakens those channels and can create overshooting; robust rules therefore balance stimulus against subsequent instability. The single-shock discussion provides useful intuition for the stochastic rankings. The exposition is competent rather than exceptional because the key numerical mechanisms and implementation details are largely deferred to an appendix.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Section IV explicitly organizes the lesson around two requirements: providing sufficient stimulus at the ELB and avoiding excessive output and inflation overshoots after liftoff. Tables 1 and 2 then compare the same rules under MCE and MCAP, linking the narrative to the quantitative exercise.

CS_Expert.layman_translation: The paper asks which promises to keep interest rates low for longer would work when rates cannot be cut below zero, especially if households and firms do not fully believe the new policy. Its simulations suggest that limited make-up strategies can outperform ordinary interest-rate rules without causing large later inflation. However, the manuscript does not provide enough code, model details, or uncertainty estimates for another researcher to rerun the experiment and verify that the reported ranking is robust.
CS_Expert.source_evidence: The manuscript states that it conducted "500 simulations of FRB/US, drawing shocks from those realized over the period 1970-2015 (i.e., bootstrapping residuals of the model)," with each simulation lasting 200 quarters and the first 100 used as burn-in. It provides no further bootstrap algorithm. It says, "For algebraic details and additional references, see the online appendix," and similarly places the detailed single-shock figures there, leaving essential rule definitions outside the supplied manuscript. Tables 1 and 2 report point estimates without Monte Carlo uncertainty. Some rankings are close: under MCE, the Reifschneider-Williams and one-year temporary PLT losses are 8.0 and 8.5, respectively. The table notes describe results as "500 simulations of 100 quarters each," whereas the text describes 200-quarter simulations with 100 reported quarters; this is plausibly shorthand for the retained sample but should be made explicit in replication documentation.

Policymaker.structural_strength: The paper tightly links a policy problem to a transparent comparative exercise: ten monetary-policy rules are evaluated in the same FRB/US environment, under the same shocks, loss function, neutral nominal rate, inflation target, and effective lower bound. It also explicitly separates macroeconomic stabilization results from communication and regime-change considerations rather than presenting the numerically best rule as an unconditional recommendation.
Policymaker.domain_audit: The actual result is narrower than the headline claim about imperfect credibility. The simulations compare full model-consistent expectations with MCAP, under which financial-market participants still fully understand and believe the policy rule while nonfinancial expectations are generated by a fixed VAR and are assumed not to change with the rule. This is a useful transition-regime stress test, but it does not represent imperfect central-bank credibility generally, especially because fully credible asset-market expectations preserve the bond-yield, equity-price, and exchange-rate channels central to lower-for-longer policy. Accordingly, the evidence supports the conditional claim that several lower-for-longer rules remain effective under this particular asymmetric expectations specification, not the broader conclusion that their advantages survive imperfect credibility. The institutional implications are otherwise responsibly limited: the paper acknowledges communication, framework-change costs, financial risks, and model dependence, and it does not claim to establish legal or administrative infeasibility. Fiscal interactions, political durability, balance-sheet consequences, and alternative welfare weights are not evaluated, so the simulations should not be framed as sufficient evidence for adoption or for ranking implementable Federal Reserve frameworks.
Policymaker.best_case_contribution: The paper provides a policy-relevant, internally consistent FRB/US comparison showing that some lower-for-longer strategies, particularly short-memory temporary price-level targeting and shadow-rate rules, can improve inflation-output stabilization relative to Taylor rules even when nonfinancial expectations do not adjust to the new regime, while more aggressive flexible price-level targeting can generate damaging volatility or overshooting. This identifies a useful design principle: robust ELB policy must balance sufficient accommodation against post-liftoff overshooting.
Policymaker.minimum_viable_revision: Narrow the abstract, introduction, and conclusion from claims about imperfect credibility generally to claims about robustness under the specific MCAP expectations structure. Explicitly state that asset-market credibility remains complete under MCAP, that the exercise does not establish robustness to partial or time-varying financial-market credibility, and that the reported loss function does not incorporate financial-stability, fiscal, distributional, communication, governance, or political-durability costs. Present the policy ranking as conditional simulation evidence rather than an implementation recommendation.
Policymaker.severity_rationale: The simulations and table comparisons appear internally coherent, so the concern is not that the model results are mathematically invalid. However, the paper's principal stated finding is explicitly about imperfect credibility, while its alternative regime retains full credibility among asset-market participants and mechanically fixes other expectations. Because credibility is central to both the motivation and conclusion, readers of the abstract or introduction could materially overgeneralize the evidence. A substantial narrowing of the headline interpretation is therefore necessary, but no new model or data are required to preserve the narrower contribution.

novelty_claims.description: A comparative policy simulation of multiple lower-for-longer rules in FRB/US under both economy-wide model-consistent expectations and an asymmetric MCAP expectations regime, emphasizing which rules remain stabilizing when nonfinancial expectations do not adjust to the policy framework.
novelty_claims.supporting_evidence: The manuscript distinguishes its exercise from Kiley and Roberts (2017), which used model-consistent expectations, and applies both MCE and MCAP to ten policy rules. The ingredients are largely established: Eggertsson and Woodford (2003) motivate price-level targeting, Reifschneider and Williams supply one shadow-rate approach, Kiley and Roberts supply another, and Reifschneider and Roberts (2006) previously discussed the expectations assumptions. The contribution is therefore a useful, bounded synthesis and quantitative policy comparison rather than a new monetary-policy mechanism or simulation method.

insight_assessment.description: The paper has a clear policy architecture and supplies useful intuition for why some lower-for-longer rules are more robust than others. Its distinction between insufficient ELB stimulus and excessive post-ELB overshooting makes the simulation rankings economically intelligible. The exposition is effective but does not provide a full institutional theory of credibility or implementation.
insight_assessment.supporting_evidence: Sections II and III organize ten rules into baseline, flexible price-level-targeting, threshold, and shadow-rate families. Section IV uses the large demand shock and Figure 1 to distill two criteria for robust frameworks: sufficient stimulus at the ELB and avoidance of excessive inflation and output overshoots. The conclusion also notes communication and framework-change costs, although these are not incorporated in the simulations.

Policymaker.layman_translation: The simulations suggest that promising to keep rates low for longer can outperform ordinary Taylor rules when rates cannot fall below zero. Some simple, limited make-up strategies work well even when households and firms do not immediately change their expectations. But the paper has not shown that these policies work whenever the central bank lacks credibility, because its skeptical-expectations case still assumes financial markets fully understand and believe the new rule. The policy conclusion should therefore be stated more narrowly.
Policymaker.source_evidence: The headline conclusion states: "imperfect credibility of the policy regime reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of using 'lower-for-longer' policies." Yet MCAP is defined so that "bond yields, equity prices, and the exchange rate are determined in a forward-looking manner," while nonfinancial forecasts "are assumed not to change when the policy rule changes." The paper itself says lower-for-longer accommodation operates through lower bond yields, higher expected inflation, and greater optimism about future growth, making retained asset-market credibility consequential. Tables 1 and 2 show that results are highly regime- and rule-dependent: inertial flexible price-level targeting's loss rises from 21.8 under MCE to 60.3 under MCAP, while the Kiley-Roberts change rule records losses of 5.7 and 5.3. The conclusion appropriately concedes that the results are not definitive and that policy choice also depends on model specification, parameter values, communication, and the costs of changing an established framework.

Theorist.referee_acknowledgment: The review graph converges on a coherent assessment: the common-model comparison is well designed conceptually and yields useful conditional rankings, but the manuscript overgeneralizes MCAP as imperfect credibility and omits enough computational detail to prevent independent auditing of the numerical results.

defenses.argument: The absence of Monte Carlo uncertainty particularly weakens close rankings, such as losses of 8.0 versus 8.5 under MCE, but it does not by itself place the broad headline comparison in doubt. Several contrasts are large—for example, under MCAP the losses are 15.2 for the Taylor rule, 10.7 for one-year temporary price-level targeting, 5.3 for the Kiley-Roberts rule, and 60.3 for inertial flexible price-level targeting. Thus uncertainty estimates may qualify fine rankings without necessarily overturning the broader finding that the performance of lower-for-longer rules varies substantially by design.

concessions.reason: I concede that the supplied manuscript is not computationally auditable. Exact rule equations, the FRB/US vintage, bootstrap dependence structure, solution algorithms, initialization, convergence diagnostics, and simulation uncertainty are absent or deferred to an unavailable appendix. Because the paper's evidence is entirely simulation-based, supplying an executable specification and uncertainty diagnostics is a substantive revision requirement, even though the omission does not demonstrate that the reported calculations are incorrect.

I agree that MCAP preserves complete understanding and belief among asset-market participants, including the forward-looking channels central to lower-for-longer policy. The evidence therefore supports robustness under one asymmetric, invariant-expectations specification rather than robustness to imperfect credibility generally. The policy conclusions must also remain conditional on the narrow stabilization loss function, which omits communication, financial-stability, fiscal, distributional, and governance costs.

Theorist.final_argument_state: The paper has a disciplined conceptual simulation design and a useful economic interpretation: effective ELB rules must balance adequate accommodation against post-liftoff overshooting. Its novelty and insight are both MEDIUM, deriving mainly from the common FRB/US comparison of ten established policy designs across two expectations specifications. Two issues survive. First, MCAP is a persistent hybrid-expectations stress test, not a general model of imperfect credibility or regime transition: financial participants remain fully credible, nonfinancial forecasts are invariant to the rule, and no learning occurs despite evaluation after a 100-quarter burn-in. The headline conclusion therefore requires substantial narrowing. Second, essential computational specifications and Monte Carlo uncertainty are missing, preventing independent audit and requiring repair within the existing framework. The broad comparisons may survive because many loss differences are sizable, but precise rankings cannot presently be verified. These are repairable issues, so resubmission rather than rejection is appropriate.

CS_Expert.referee_acknowledgment: The peer reviews correctly identify the paper's central interpretive limitation: MCAP is a specific asymmetric expectations specification, not a general model of imperfect credibility or transition learning. That concern complements the computational audit, which finds the reported quantitative rankings insufficiently reproducible and lacking simulation uncertainty.

attacks.critique: The central numerical evidence cannot be independently audited from the supplied manuscript because essential elements of the computational experiment are unspecified. The exact policy-rule equations, FRB/US vintage, residual series, bootstrap dependence structure, initialization, expectations-solution algorithms, random seeds, convergence criteria, and failed-run handling are absent. Point estimates are also reported without Monte Carlo uncertainty, leaving close rule rankings unsupported.
attacks.evidence: Section I states only that 500 simulations bootstrap FRB/US residuals from 1970–2015, with 200 quarters per simulation and a 100-quarter burn-in. It does not say whether equation residuals are resampled jointly, whether temporal blocks are used, or how residual dates are aligned. Section II defers algebraic definitions to an online appendix not included in the supplied manuscript. Tables 1 and 2 provide no Monte Carlo standard errors or repeated-seed intervals, even though some comparisons are close, including MCE losses of 8.0 for Reifschneider-Williams and 8.5 for one-year temporary price-level targeting.

attacks.critique: The headline conclusion generalizes too broadly from MCAP to imperfect credibility. MCAP preserves complete understanding and belief among asset-market participants while fixing nonfinancial expectations to a forecasting system that never adapts to the policy rule. It therefore tests robustness to one persistent hybrid-expectations regime, not imperfect credibility generally or a transition involving learning.
attacks.evidence: The manuscript defines MCAP so that bond yields, equity prices, and exchange rates remain forward-looking, whereas expectations of income, inflation, and other nonfinancial variables are based on a small VAR and are assumed not to change when the policy rule changes. Nevertheless, the conclusion states that imperfect credibility reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies. Moreover, the simulations discard a 100-quarter burn-in and evaluate a subsequent 100 quarters without specifying any learning or convergence mechanism.

concessions.reason: I agree that MCAP should be described as a persistent hybrid or invariant-expectations stress test rather than a general model of imperfect credibility or regime-transition dynamics. The long burn-in without learning makes the transition interpretation especially difficult to sustain.

I agree that the policy implications must remain conditional on full asset-market credibility, the FRB/US specification, and the narrow inflation-output loss function. The exercise does not establish robustness to partial financial-market credibility or incorporate communication, financial-stability, fiscal, distributional, governance, or political-durability costs.

CS_Expert.final_argument_state: The experimental comparison is conceptually disciplined, and the broad economic insight—that effective lower-for-longer rules must balance ELB accommodation against post-liftoff overshooting—is useful. Novelty and insight are both MEDIUM: the contribution is a common-model comparison across established policy rules and two expectations specifications, rather than a new mechanism or computational method. However, execution is not adequately auditable because essential model, rule, bootstrap, and solution details are absent and no Monte Carlo uncertainty accompanies the rankings. In addition, the central imperfect-credibility claim requires substantial narrowing to the specific MCAP hybrid-expectations stress test. Both defects are repairable within the current framework through complete computational documentation, uncertainty reporting, and claim recalibration, so resubmission rather than rejection is appropriate.

Policymaker.referee_acknowledgment: The reviews converge on the paper's useful controlled comparison and medium policy contribution. The principal unresolved issues are whether MCAP warrants the headline language of imperfect credibility and whether incomplete computational documentation constitutes an argument-damaging substantive flaw rather than a transparency deficiency.

attacks.critique: The central conclusion generalizes beyond the expectations experiment actually conducted. MCAP preserves complete understanding and belief in the policy rule among asset-market participants while fixing nonfinancial forecasts to a VAR that does not respond to the regime. Because lower-for-longer policy operates importantly through bond yields and other asset prices, this specification does not establish robustness to imperfect credibility generally.
attacks.evidence: The manuscript defines MCAP by making bond yields, equity prices, and exchange rates forward-looking while assuming expectations of income, inflation, and other nonfinancial variables do not change with the policy rule. Nevertheless, the conclusion states broadly that imperfect credibility reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies.

defenses.argument: The missing equations, bootstrap details, code, and Monte Carlo uncertainty materially limit independent auditability and should be remedied. However, the manuscript does not base its main conclusion on the close 8.0-versus-8.5 loss comparison. Its broader findings concern substantially larger contrasts, such as Taylor versus one-year temporary price-level targeting and the severe deterioration of flexible price-level targeting under MCAP. Without affirmative evidence of an incorrect implementation or uncertainty large enough to overturn those broad comparisons, the documentation deficit alone does not establish an argument-damaging substantive flaw in the computed work. It is best treated as a serious replication and reporting revision accompanying the central claim recalibration.

concessions.reason: The transition interpretation is overstated because the simulations discard a 100-quarter burn-in and then evaluate another 100 quarters without learning or convergence in nonfinancial expectations. The paper therefore demonstrates robustness to a persistent asymmetric expectations stress test, not transition dynamics or imperfect credibility in general.

The supplied manuscript is not independently reproducible: essential rule equations and computational details are deferred to an unavailable appendix, and no Monte Carlo uncertainty is reported. These omissions require substantial documentation, replication materials, and qualification of close numerical rankings.

questions.question: Is there manuscript evidence that simulation uncertainty or bootstrap implementation could plausibly reverse the broad Taylor-rule versus short-memory temporary-PLT comparison, rather than only close rankings such as losses of 8.0 versus 8.5?

Would replacing credibility and transition language with a precise description of MCAP as a persistent hybrid-expectations stress test fully resolve the interpretation problem without new simulations?

Policymaker.final_argument_state: The conditional simulation exercise appears internally coherent and policy-relevant, but its central interpretation must be narrowed. The surviving result is that, within the stated FRB/US calibration, several short-memory temporary price-level-targeting and shadow-rate rules outperform Taylor rules under both economy-wide model-consistent expectations and one specific asymmetric expectations specification. It does not establish robustness to imperfect credibility generally, partial financial-market belief, or learning during regime transition. Computational documentation and Monte Carlo uncertainty should also be added, especially before asserting close rankings, although the manuscript provides no direct evidence that these omissions overturn the broad comparisons. Novelty is MEDIUM because the contribution is a common-model synthesis across established rules and expectations specifications. Insight is MEDIUM because the stimulus-versus-overshooting tradeoff is clear and useful but not a full theory of credibility or implementation. The central overclaim requires substantial rephrasing, so the appropriate verdict is RESUBMIT.

Theorist.referee_acknowledgment: The review graph has converged on a coherent assessment: the comparative simulation design is useful, but the imperfect-credibility interpretation is too broad and the supplied manuscript lacks essential information needed to audit its numerical evidence.

attacks.critique: The manuscript's headline claim about imperfect credibility exceeds the experiment conducted. MCAP assumes that asset-market participants fully understand and believe each policy rule, while nonfinancial expectations follow a fixed forecasting specification that does not adapt to the regime. This is a persistent asymmetric-expectations stress test, not a general model of imperfect credibility or transition to a newly announced regime.
attacks.evidence: The manuscript states that bond yields, equity prices, and exchange rates are determined with model-consistent expectations under MCAP, whereas expectations of income, inflation, and other nonfinancial variables are based on a small VAR and are assumed not to change when the policy rule changes. Nevertheless, Sections III and V characterize the findings as showing that imperfect credibility generally reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies. The transition interpretation is particularly strained because outcomes are evaluated after a 100-quarter burn-in without any specified learning mechanism.

attacks.critique: The central simulation evidence is not independently auditable from the supplied manuscript. Exact rule definitions and essential implementation choices are missing, while no simulation uncertainty is reported. This does not establish that the broad comparisons are wrong, but it prevents verification of the experiment and leaves close rankings unsupported.
attacks.evidence: Section II sends the algebraic definitions to an unavailable online appendix. Section I says that residuals from 1970–2015 are bootstrapped but does not specify joint versus equation-wise resampling, temporal dependence, residual alignment, initialization, the FRB/US vintage, solution procedures, convergence diagnostics, or failed-run treatment. Tables 1 and 2 report only point estimates, even for close MCE loss comparisons such as 8.0 for Reifschneider-Williams versus 8.5 for one-year temporary price-level targeting.

attacks.critique: Classifying the computational omissions principally as an extension understates their role. Executable replication code could be viewed as an additional transparency measure, but the exact equations, bootstrap construction, solution method, and uncertainty attached to simulated rankings are part of defining and validating the reported experiment itself.
attacks.evidence: All quantitative conclusions arise from stochastic FRB/US simulations, yet the supplied manuscript does not contain enough information to reconstruct those simulations. Large tabulated contrasts make the broad qualitative conclusions more plausible, but they do not substitute for a complete specification of the computational experiment.

defenses.argument: The lack of Monte Carlo uncertainty most directly undermines close rankings rather than every qualitative comparison. Several loss differences are large, including MCAP losses of 15.2 for the Taylor rule, 10.7 for one-year temporary price-level targeting, 5.3 for the Kiley-Roberts rule, and 60.3 for inertial flexible price-level targeting. Thus the documentation and uncertainty defect requires substantive repair, but the manuscript supplies no affirmative basis for concluding that all broad lower-for-longer comparisons would be overturned.

The existence of large contrasts supports preserving the paper's broad comparative result, but it does not make specification and uncertainty reporting optional. Exact policy equations and simulation design choices determine the estimand being compared and therefore belong to the work's core methodological documentation rather than solely to future replication infrastructure.

concessions.reason: I agree that MCAP does not establish robustness to imperfect credibility generally. It preserves full credibility in the financial-market channel most important for lower-for-longer policy and imposes invariant nonfinancial forecasting behavior without learning.

I agree that the policy implications must remain conditional on the FRB/US specification, full asset-market credibility under MCAP, and a narrow loss function containing only inflation and output-gap stabilization. The exercise does not incorporate communication, financial-stability, fiscal, distributional, governance, or political-durability costs.

questions.question: How are FRB/US residuals resampled across equations and time, and how sensitive are the rule rankings to alternative bootstrap designs and repeated simulation seeds?
Can the authors report Monte Carlo intervals for each loss difference and explicitly distinguish statistically stable broad comparisons from numerically close rankings?
What conception of regime transition justifies interpreting MCAP as transitional when nonfinancial agents never learn and evaluation begins only after a 100-quarter burn-in?

Theorist.final_argument_state: The paper presents a disciplined and policy-relevant comparison of ten established monetary-policy rules in a common FRB/US framework. Its central economic insight—that robust lower-for-longer policies must provide sufficient ELB accommodation without generating excessive post-liftoff overshooting—is clear and useful. Novelty is MEDIUM because the contribution is primarily the common-model comparison across policy designs and two expectations specifications rather than a new policy mechanism or theory. Insight is MEDIUM because the stimulus-versus-overshooting tradeoff is informative but does not amount to a general theory of credibility or regime transition. Two repairable issues survive. First, MCAP supports robustness only under a particular persistent hybrid-expectations specification, so the central imperfect-credibility and transition claims require substantial narrowing. Second, missing equations, computational specifications, and simulation uncertainty prevent independent audit and qualification of close rankings. Large loss differences mean the broad comparative findings may survive these repairs, but the supplied evidence is not yet adequately documented. Resubmission is therefore appropriate.

CS_Expert.referee_acknowledgment: The review graph converges on two principal issues: incomplete computational auditability and overgeneralization from MCAP to imperfect credibility broadly. I agree that neither issue establishes that the reported broad numerical patterns are false, but both require repair before the paper's central conclusions can be accepted as stated.

attacks.critique: Characterizing the missing computational specification as merely a replication and reporting issue understates its importance. Because the paper's evidentiary contribution consists entirely of simulated comparisons, unavailable rule equations and unspecified bootstrap and solution procedures prevent verification that the reported outcomes implement the stated policy regimes. This places the numerical evidence in substantive doubt even though it does not affirmatively show that the calculations are wrong.
attacks.evidence: Section II defers the algebraic definitions of all policy rules to an unavailable online appendix. Section I does not identify the FRB/US vintage, explain whether residual vectors are resampled jointly or in temporal blocks, describe the expectations-solution algorithms, or report failed-run handling and convergence diagnostics. Tables 1 and 2 provide only point estimates from 500 simulations. Thus neither the policy mappings nor their computed loss comparisons can be independently reconstructed from the supplied manuscript.

defenses.argument: Large reported loss differences make it plausible that some qualitative comparisons would survive ordinary Monte Carlo error, but point-estimate separation alone does not address uncertainty from residual resampling, simulation dependence, initialization, or systematic implementation choices. My objection therefore concerns auditability and support for rankings, not an assertion that every broad lower-for-longer comparison would be overturned.

The absence of affirmative evidence of coding error is not sufficient when the manuscript does not provide the equations and computational information needed to check the simulation experiment. Since all quantitative support comes from that experiment, complete within-framework documentation and uncertainty diagnostics are necessary evidentiary repairs rather than optional extensions.

concessions.reason: I agree that missing Monte Carlo uncertainty does not by itself invalidate the broad contrasts with very large reported loss differences. Its most immediate effect is to leave close rankings, such as MCE losses of 8.0 versus 8.5, unsupported; the missing equations and implementation details create the more general auditability problem.

I agree that the paper contains no direct evidence that incomplete documentation has reversed the broad comparisons. The defect is repairable by supplying an executable specification, replication materials, and uncertainty diagnostics, so it warrants resubmission rather than rejection.

Will the authors replace the general imperfect-credibility and regime-transition interpretation with the narrower claim that the rules are tested under a persistent hybrid specification featuring full asset-market credibility and invariant VAR-based nonfinancial expectations?

CS_Expert.final_argument_state: The paper offers a coherent and useful simulation comparison whose main economic insight is that lower-for-longer rules must balance adequate ELB stimulus against subsequent inflation and output overshooting. Novelty is MEDIUM because the contribution is primarily a common FRB/US evaluation of established policy rules under two expectations specifications. Insight is MEDIUM because the stimulus-versus-overshooting interpretation is informative but does not constitute a general account of credibility or learning. Two decision-relevant issues survive. First, the simulation evidence is not independently auditable from the supplied manuscript because exact rule equations and essential model, bootstrap, solution, and uncertainty information are absent; this is a repairable substantive flaw, particularly damaging to precise rankings. Second, the headline imperfect-credibility conclusion requires substantial rephrasing because MCAP is a persistent asymmetric expectations stress test, not a general model of partial credibility or regime-transition learning. These repairs fit within the existing framework, supporting RESUBMIT rather than rejection.

Policymaker.referee_acknowledgment: The review graph correctly converges on two principal issues: the manuscript's broad interpretation of MCAP as imperfect credibility or regime transition, and the inadequate auditability of an entirely simulation-based exercise. The former is a central claim-calibration problem; the latter requires substantive computational documentation and uncertainty analysis.

attacks.critique: The headline conclusion overgeneralizes from a highly specific asymmetric-expectations experiment. MCAP assumes that asset-market participants fully understand and believe the policy rule, while nonfinancial expectations follow an invariant VAR and never learn. Because lower-for-longer policy works importantly through forward-looking asset prices, these simulations do not establish robustness to imperfect credibility generally or to an actual regime transition.
attacks.evidence: The manuscript states that bond yields, equity prices, and exchange rates are determined with model-consistent expectations under MCAP, whereas expectations of inflation, income, and other nonfinancial variables do not change when the policy rule changes. It nevertheless concludes broadly that imperfect credibility reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies. The 100-quarter burn-in and subsequent 100-quarter evaluation contain no learning mechanism, further undermining the claimed transition interpretation.

attacks.critique: The central numerical evidence is insufficiently auditable and its close rankings are not statistically supported. Since all substantive results come from stochastic FRB/US simulations, omitting exact policy-rule equations, bootstrap and solution details, model vintage, failure handling, and Monte Carlo uncertainty prevents verification of implementation and precision.
attacks.evidence: Section I reports 500 simulations, residual bootstrapping from 1970–2015, 200-quarter paths, and a 100-quarter burn-in, but does not specify joint versus equation-by-equation resampling, temporal dependence, initialization, solution algorithms, convergence diagnostics, or failed-run treatment. Section II defers exact rule definitions to an unavailable appendix. Tables 1 and 2 report point estimates without Monte Carlo standard errors or intervals, including close MCE loss comparisons such as 8.0 versus 8.5.

defenses.argument: The lack of Monte Carlo uncertainty does not itself demonstrate that the broad qualitative comparisons are wrong. Several reported differences are large—for example, MCAP losses of 15.2 for the Taylor rule, 10.7 for one-year temporary price-level targeting, 5.3 for the Kiley-Roberts rule, and 60.3 for inertial flexible price-level targeting. Uncertainty estimates are essential for close rankings and verification, but absent evidence of very large simulation error, the broad conclusion that lower-for-longer designs perform quite differently need not be discarded.

concessions.reason: I concede that the documentation deficit is substantive rather than merely an optional extension. Because the evidence is wholly computational, the exact rule definitions, model and bootstrap specifications, solution procedures, diagnostics, replication materials, and uncertainty estimates are necessary to audit whether the reported results follow from the stated experiment.

I agree that MCAP is best characterized as a persistent hybrid-expectations stress test. Full asset-market belief preserves a central transmission channel, while invariant nonfinancial forecasts and the absence of learning prevent the exercise from representing imperfect credibility or regime-transition dynamics generally.

questions.question: Do the qualitative rule comparisons and reported loss rankings survive repeated random seeds, alternative residual-resampling schemes, and confidence intervals that account for dependence within simulated paths?

Can the authors restate the principal result explicitly as conditional on full asset-market credibility, invariant VAR-based nonfinancial expectations, the FRB/US specification, and the stated inflation-output stabilization loss?

Policymaker.final_argument_state: The manuscript presents an internally coherent and policy-relevant comparison of established monetary-policy rules, and its core economic intuition—that robust lower-for-longer designs must balance ELB stimulus against post-liftoff overshooting—is useful. Novelty is MEDIUM because the contribution is principally a common FRB/US comparison of ten existing rule designs under two expectations specifications. Insight is MEDIUM because the accommodation-versus-overshooting tradeoff is clearly developed, but the exercise does not supply a general theory or realistic transition model of credibility. The surviving result is conditional: within the stated calibration, several short-memory temporary price-level-targeting and shadow-rate rules outperform Taylor rules under both economy-wide model-consistent expectations and one asymmetric hybrid-expectations stress test. The paper does not establish robustness to imperfect credibility generally, partial asset-market belief, or learning during regime transition. Complete computational specifications, replication materials, and Monte Carlo uncertainty are also required, particularly before maintaining close rankings. These defects are repairable within the existing framework, so the appropriate verdict is RESUBMIT.

final_report.editorial_rationale_and_integration:
Decision: MAJOR REVISION REQUIRED. The strongest credible version of the paper is a controlled FRB/US comparison of ten established monetary-policy rules under a common calibration, shock history, effective lower bound, loss criterion, and two expectations specifications. Its useful substantive contribution is to show that lower-for-longer designs are not interchangeable: within this environment, short-memory temporary price-level targeting and shadow-rate rules can provide accommodation at the ELB while avoiding the severe post-liftoff overshooting associated with some flexible price-level-targeting rules. The aggregate-demand exercise gives the rankings a clear economic interpretation. Novelty is MEDIUM because the principal addition is a common quantitative comparison across established rules and expectations specifications, rather than a new model, mechanism, or computational method. Insight is also MEDIUM: the accommodation-versus-overshooting tradeoff is clear and policy-relevant, but the paper does not develop a general theory of credibility or transition dynamics.

The principal substantive flaw is computational auditability. All central evidence comes from stochastic FRB/US simulations, yet the supplied manuscript does not identify the exact model vintage and coefficient set, state all policy-rule equations, or adequately document the residual bootstrap, including joint versus equation-wise resampling, temporal dependence, and residual-date alignment. It also omits initialization details, expectations-solution algorithms, convergence criteria, failed-run treatment, and reproducible computational materials. The text describes 200-quarter paths with a 100-quarter burn-in, while the table notes refer to 500 simulations of 100 quarters; this may simply describe the retained sample, but it must be made unambiguous. Finally, the tables report point estimates without Monte Carlo standard errors or repeated-seed intervals. Large contrasts make some broad qualitative findings plausible, but they do not substitute for a complete specification of the experiment, and close comparisons such as losses of 8.0 and 8.5 under MCE cannot presently support a precise ranking.

A separate substantial-rephrasal issue concerns the central credibility claim. MCAP is not a general model of imperfect credibility: asset-market participants retain model-consistent expectations and understand the policy rule, while expectations of income, inflation, and other nonfinancial variables follow a small VAR and are imposed not to change with the rule. Nor does the exercise model transition learning, despite describing MCAP as transitional and evaluating outcomes after a long burn-in. The evidence therefore supports robustness under a particular persistent hybrid or invariant-nonfinancial-expectations stress test, not the general conclusion that imperfect credibility reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies. This distinction is central because forward-looking asset prices are an important transmission channel for those policies.

The critiques that should not be overstated are equally important. The record contains no affirmative evidence that the calculations are wrong or that ordinary Monte Carlo error would reverse every broad comparison. Several reported differences are large, including the poor MCAP performance of inertial flexible price-level targeting and the stronger performance of the Kiley-Roberts rule. The appropriate response is therefore repair and qualification, not rejection of the entire exercise. Likewise, broader issues involving financial stability, fiscal interactions, distribution, governance, communication, and political durability are limitations or future extensions rather than demands for a new paper. They should delimit policy interpretation, not be treated as required new modeling. No separate minor-rephrasal issues were identified beyond the central recalibration and clarification of simulation length.
final_report.official_letter_to_the_author:
Dear Authors,

The paper addresses an important policy question through a disciplined common-model comparison. Evaluating ten rules in the same FRB/US environment makes the differences among lower-for-longer strategies unusually transparent. The most promising result is not that all such strategies dominate conventional rules, but that their design matters: short-memory temporary price-level targeting and shadow-rate approaches appear to balance ELB accommodation against subsequent inflation and output overshooting more successfully than some flexible price-level-targeting alternatives. The aggregate-demand experiment provides useful intuition for this result.

After considering the manuscript and the unanimous referee assessments, my decision is MAJOR REVISION REQUIRED. There are no unresolvable blockers, and the concerns can be addressed within the paper's existing framework. Two revisions are essential.

First, the quantitative evidence must become independently auditable. Please identify the exact FRB/US vintage, data, and coefficient set; provide the algebraic definition and state variables of every policy rule; and document the MCE and MCAP solution procedures. The residual bootstrap must specify whether residuals are sampled jointly across equations, whether temporal blocks are used, how dates are aligned, and how cross-equation and serial dependence are preserved. Please also report initialization, random seeds, convergence criteria, diagnostics, and the treatment of failed simulations. Clarify that each path contains 200 quarters, of which the first 100 are burn-in and the second 100 form the reported sample, if that is indeed the procedure. A replication package or equivalently complete executable specification should reproduce Tables 1 and 2.

Please also quantify simulation uncertainty. Report Monte Carlo standard errors, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed intervals for the table statistics and relevant loss differences. Distinguish broad comparisons that are stable from close rankings that cannot be resolved at the available precision. The absence of these measures does not establish that the broad findings are false, but it currently prevents readers from assessing their numerical reliability.

Second, the interpretation of MCAP must be narrowed throughout the abstract, introduction, results, and conclusion. Under MCAP, asset-market participants continue to understand and believe the policy rule, while nonfinancial expectations are generated by a fixed VAR and do not respond to the regime. This is a useful asymmetric or hybrid-expectations stress test, but it is not a general representation of imperfect credibility. It also does not describe transition learning, because no learning mechanism is specified and the reported sample follows a 100-quarter burn-in. The principal conclusion should therefore state that selected lower-for-longer rules retain advantages under this particular expectations specification, conditional on the FRB/US calibration and loss function. Please distinguish credibility in financial markets from the forecasting technology imposed on other agents.

The policy discussion should likewise remain conditional. The simulations compare inflation-output stabilization under the stated model and do not incorporate financial-stability, fiscal, distributional, communication, governance, or political-durability costs. These omissions do not require a major expansion of the model, but they preclude presenting the simulated ranking as sufficient evidence for implementation. Your existing acknowledgment of communication and framework-change costs is a good foundation for this qualification.

The revision need not introduce a new learning or partial-credibility model to preserve the paper's core contribution. Such analysis would be a valuable extension, but the minimum acceptable revision is to describe MCAP precisely, recalibrate the claims, fully specify the computational experiment, and report its numerical uncertainty. If those changes confirm the broad patterns, the paper would offer a useful and appropriately bounded contribution.

Sincerely,
Senior Coordinating Editor
final_report.minimum_viable_revision_path:
1. Recast MCAP everywhere as a specific persistent hybrid-expectations stress test: full model-consistent expectations for asset prices combined with invariant VAR-based expectations for nonfinancial variables. Remove general claims about imperfect credibility and regime-transition learning unless additional modeling directly supports them.

2. Restate the principal finding conditionally: within the specified FRB/US calibration, neutral nominal rate, ELB, expectations structures, and inflation-output loss function, some short-memory temporary price-level-targeting and shadow-rate rules outperform Taylor rules and avoid the overshooting generated by some flexible price-level-targeting rules.

3. Put all essential policy-rule equations and state-variable definitions in the manuscript or a supplied, permanent appendix. Readers must be able to reconstruct all ten policy mappings.

4. Fully document the computational experiment: exact FRB/US vintage and inputs; residual series; joint/equation-wise and temporal bootstrap design; residual alignment; initialization; random seeds; MCE and MCAP solution algorithms; convergence criteria; diagnostics; and failed-run handling.

5. Resolve the simulation-length wording by explicitly distinguishing the 200-quarter generated paths, 100-quarter burn-in, and 100-quarter retained evaluation sample.

6. Supply executable replication materials, or an equivalently complete specification, that reproduce Tables 1 and 2.

7. Add Monte Carlo standard errors or repeated-seed confidence intervals for all reported statistics and relevant pairwise loss differences. Qualify or avoid precise rankings when differences, including 8.0 versus 8.5 under MCE, are not distinguishable at the reported precision.

8. State that the policy ranking excludes financial-stability, fiscal, distributional, communication, governance, and political-durability costs. Treat modeling partial credibility or gradual learning as valuable future work, not as a condition for the minimum revision.
final_report.constructive_summary: The paper has a credible and useful core: a common FRB/US comparison showing that the design of lower-for-longer policy matters, with robust performance requiring enough ELB stimulus but not excessive post-liftoff overshooting. Its novelty and insight are moderate rather than foundational, but the policy synthesis is promising. The present manuscript cannot yet sustain its conclusions because the simulation pipeline is insufficiently specified and its numerical uncertainty is unreported. In addition, MCAP supports a narrower conditional result than the headline claim about imperfect credibility or regime transition. A focused revision that makes the experiment reproducible, reports Monte Carlo precision, and recalibrates the credibility language can preserve the existing numerical analysis and substantially strengthen the paper.

Moreover, the simulations discard a 100-quarter burn-in and evaluate a subsequent 100 quarters without specifying any learning or convergence mechanism.

debate_nodes.evidence: The manuscript states that bond yields, equity prices, and exchange rates are determined with model-consistent expectations under MCAP, whereas expectations of income, inflation, and other nonfinancial variables are based on a small VAR and are assumed not to change when the policy rule changes. Nevertheless, Sections III and V characterize the findings as showing that imperfect credibility generally reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies. The transition interpretation is particularly strained because outcomes are evaluated after a 100-quarter burn-in without any specified learning mechanism.

debate_nodes.evidence: Section II sends the algebraic definitions to an unavailable online appendix. Section I says that residuals from 1970–2015 are bootstrapped but does not specify joint versus equation-wise resampling, temporal dependence, residual alignment, initialization, the FRB/US vintage, solution procedures, convergence diagnostics, or failed-run treatment. Tables 1 and 2 report only point estimates, even for close MCE loss comparisons such as 8.0 for Reifschneider-Williams versus 8.5 for one-year temporary price-level targeting.

debate_nodes.evidence: All quantitative conclusions arise from stochastic FRB/US simulations, yet the supplied manuscript does not contain enough information to reconstruct those simulations. Large tabulated contrasts make the broad qualitative conclusions more plausible, but they do not substitute for a complete specification of the computational experiment.
debate_nodes.outcome_reason: No matching defense was recorded; treated as unresolved rather than conceded.

debate_nodes.evidence: Section II defers the algebraic definitions of all policy rules to an unavailable online appendix. Section I does not identify the FRB/US vintage, explain whether residual vectors are resampled jointly or in temporal blocks, describe the expectations-solution algorithms, or report failed-run handling and convergence diagnostics. Tables 1 and 2 provide only point estimates from 500 simulations. Thus neither the policy mappings nor their computed loss comparisons can be independently reconstructed from the supplied manuscript.

The manuscript states that bond yields, equity prices, and exchange rates are determined with model-consistent expectations under MCAP, whereas expectations of inflation, income, and other nonfinancial variables do not change when the policy rule changes. It nevertheless concludes broadly that imperfect credibility reduces but does not eliminate the advantages of lower-for-longer policies. The 100-quarter burn-in and subsequent 100-quarter evaluation contain no learning mechanism, further undermining the claimed transition interpretation.
debate_nodes.outcome_reason: Paper critique recorded; no peer defense was required.

debate_nodes.evidence: Section I reports 500 simulations, residual bootstrapping from 1970–2015, 200-quarter paths, and a 100-quarter burn-in, but does not specify joint versus equation-by-equation resampling, temporal dependence, initialization, solution algorithms, convergence diagnostics, or failed-run treatment. Section II defers exact rule definitions to an unavailable appendix. Tables 1 and 2 report point estimates without Monte Carlo standard errors or intervals, including close MCE loss comparisons such as 8.0 versus 8.5.
